endorsements.quote: At each institution, an appropriate governance committee of stakeholders, including AI and informatics experts, clinicians, and patients from various specialties, should be established to review AI systems.
Institutions should implement periodic performance audits to ensure no unexpected performance changes that could cause harm and would require de-implementing or re-training AI systems.

Thus, for medical care in which AI systems will be utilized to facilitate decision-making, operative planning, or to accomplish physical tasks, the surgeon must be sufficiently knowledgeable about the AI tool to explain it in understandable terms to the patient.

Furthermore, surgeons should be equipped to have a discussion on reasonable alternatives to not using AI assistance in a patient’s care, offering data on how care might be different or whether there are any expected differences in outcome due to not using an AI system.

Transparency is two-fold: AI developers must disclose how they use patient data to train medical AI systems, and clinicians must inform patients when AI is used to generate diagnosis or treatment recommendations [ 26 ].

This oversight includes vetting new AI models, serving as the operational home for existing ones, and conducting continuous surveillance of performance to ensure safety and effectiveness, which may involve phasing out underperforming models.

unlisted_practices: Ensure AI developers supply comprehensive user manuals, training sessions, and safety guidelines with their products.
Establish standardized credentialing and certification programs for clinicians using specific AI tools.
Partner with specialty societies for guidance on training and credentialing in specific AI tools.
Require developers of clinical AI to build guardrails specifying the clinical scenarios in which the model should and should not be used.
Appoint a Chief Health AI Officer to oversee the ecosystem of clinical AI tools within an institution.
Build point-of-care capacity, comparable to clinical pharmacists, to ensure providers use AI models safely and effectively.
Surgeons should disclose their training, qualifications, and experience with AI systems to patients.
Surgeons should describe the AI's role and safeguards, including cross-checking and overriding, to patients during informed consent.
Discuss with patients the unique risks of AI, including algorithmic bias, malfunction, and data privacy and security risks, during informed consent.
Use pre-existing specialty society multi-institutional clinical databases to facilitate post-market data sharing for assessing generalizability, effectiveness, and model drift.
Vet AI systems for the type and nature of errors they may make, not only their error rates.
Consider the necessity and feasibility of obtaining patient consent before repurposing data for AI development, distinct from consent for AI use in treatment.

screen.reason: This is a SAGES white paper/consensus statement outlining recommendations and frameworks for risk, liability, governance, and safe deployment of AI systems in surgery.
